title: Data Structures and Algorithms in Python
subtitle: Analyse, implement and test the core data structures and algorithms in Python, from hash tables and heaps to graph search and dynamic programming.
outcomes: Analyse running time and memory with Big-O, and check the analysis with doubling tests
Choose the right Python structure (list, dict, set, deque or heap) and predict what it costs
Implement and test linked lists, binary search trees and binary heaps
Solve problems with two pointers, sliding windows, stacks and binary search
Find routes with BFS and Dijkstra's algorithm, and order tasks with topological sort
Design recursive and dynamic programming solutions, and reconstruct their answers
prerequisites: Python Programming with PyCharm, or equivalent experience: functions, classes, lists, dictionaries and loops, and running pytest. School algebra (powers and logarithms) helps. Install Python 3.10 or newer and pytest (python -m pip install pytest); any editor works.
description:
Data structures and algorithms are the toolkit behind fast, dependable software: knowing what a dictionary lookup costs, when a heap beats sorting, or how to turn an exponential recursion into a quick table is what separates code that copes with real data from code that grinds to a halt. This course teaches that toolkit in Python, with analysis and testing throughout. You'll learn Big-O and check it with doubling tests, see what Python's lists, dictionaries and sets really cost, and build the classic structures yourself: linked lists, stacks and queues, binary search trees and binary heaps. Then you'll explore graphs with breadth-first and depth-first search, topological sort and Dijkstra's algorithm, and finish with sorting, binary search, recursion and dynamic programming.

Every module has a lab in which you implement the ideas and prove them with pytest, and each lab counts the work done, so you see quadratic, linear and logarithmic growth for yourself instead of taking it on trust. The capstone, a tested journey planner for a transit network, brings it all together: graph search for routes, binary search over timetables, a heap for the busiest stops and dynamic programming for the cheapest fares. The course builds on Python Programming with PyCharm; afterwards, System Design Fundamentals: Scale, Caching and Load Balancing applies these structures to whole systems, and Concurrency and Asynchronous Programming in Python covers doing work in parallel.

modules.title: Complexity, arrays and hashing
modules.summary: Learn to reason about how running time and memory grow with the input, then see what Python's lists, dictionaries and sets cost and how hashing turns slow searches into fast lookups.

lessons.title: Big-O and counting operations
objectives: Express an algorithm's running time and memory in Big-O notation
Distinguish worst-case, average-case and amortised costs
Check a growth claim with a doubling test
key_points: Big-O describes how cost grows with the input size n, ignoring constant factors and smaller terms: 3n² + 5n + 2 is O(n²). Formally, f(n) is O(g(n)) if f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for some constant c and every large enough n; Ω gives a lower bound and Θ a tight one.

The common classes, from best to worst: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n²), O(2^n) and O(n!). Doubling n doubles an O(n) cost, roughly quadruples an O(n²) cost, and adds a single step to an O(log n) cost.

Count the work in the innermost repeated step: one loop over n items is O(n), a loop inside a loop over the same items is O(n²), and halving the problem each step is O(log n). Steps in sequence add; nested steps multiply.

Worst case bounds every input; average case assumes a distribution of inputs; amortised cost averages over a sequence of operations, so an occasional expensive step, such as a list growing its storage, is spread across the many cheap ones.
Space complexity counts extra memory: building a new list of n items is O(n) space, sorting in place needs O(1) extra, and every level of recursion uses a stack frame.
Big-O hides constants, so measure too: time the code at n, 2n and 4n (a doubling test) and check that the ratios match the claim. For small n, a simple O(n²) method can beat a clever O(n log n) one.

lessons.title: Python lists as dynamic arrays
objectives: Predict the cost of common list operations
Explain why append is amortised O(1)
Avoid hidden quadratic behaviour in Python code
key_points: A Python list is a dynamic array of references stored next to each other, so a[i] and assignment to it are O(1), and len() is O(1) because the length is stored.

append is amortised O(1): when the array is full, CPython allocates a larger one with spare room (growing by a fraction of its size) and copies the references across, and these copies are rare enough to average out.

Inserting or deleting anywhere but the end shifts every later element, so insert(0, x) and pop(0) are O(n), and so is x in a, which checks items one by one. Use collections.deque for queues and a set for membership tests.
Slicing copies: a[i:j] costs O(j − i) time and memory, so slicing inside a loop, or recursing on a[1:], can turn an O(n) algorithm into an O(n²) one.
Strings are immutable, so building one with += in a loop may copy the growing string each time; collect the pieces in a list and call ''.join(pieces) once, which is O(total length).
sorted() and list.sort() are O(n log n); min, max and sum are O(n); a list comprehension is O(n) like the equivalent loop, and usually faster.

lessons.title: Hash tables: dictionaries and sets
objectives: Explain how a hash table maps keys to slots
State the average and worst-case costs of dict and set operations
Replace nested loops with dictionary and set lookups
key_points: A hash table stores entries in an array of slots: hash(key) picks a slot, and collisions (two keys wanting one slot) are resolved by probing other slots, as CPython's dict and set do (open addressing), or by chaining a list of entries in each slot.

Lookup, insertion and deletion are O(1) on average, because the table grows to keep its load factor (entries per slot) low; the worst case is O(n) when many keys collide, which a good hash function makes unlikely.

Keys must be hashable: a key's hash must never change, and objects that compare equal must have equal hashes. Immutable built-ins (int, str, frozenset, tuples of hashables) qualify; lists and dicts don't.

Python randomises the hashes of str and bytes for each process (see PYTHONHASHSEED), so the order of a set of strings can change between runs, and hash() values must never be stored or used to place data across processes.
Replace a nested loop with a lookup: two-sum checks each number's complement in a dict of the numbers seen so far, O(n) instead of comparing every pair in O(n²).
collections.Counter counts items, defaultdict(list) groups them by a key, and a set removes duplicates; all three are hash tables. Since Python 3.7, dicts keep their insertion order.

"""Doubling tests: count steps at n, 2n and 4n, and time list and set membership."""
import timeit

from counting import has_duplicate_hash, has_duplicate_quadratic, two_sum, two_sum_quadratic

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Distinct items (the worst case):")
    previous = None
    for n in (1_000, 2_000, 4_000):
        items = list(range(n))
        _, quad = has_duplicate_quadratic(items)
        _, hashed = has_duplicate_hash(items)
        ratio = "" if previous is None else f"  (x{quad / previous[0]:.2f} and x{hashed / previous[1]:.2f})"
        print(f"  n={n:>5}: pairwise {quad:>9,} comparisons, set {hashed:>5,} lookups{ratio}")
        previous = (quad, hashed)
    nums = list(range(0, 4_000, 2))                      # 2,000 even numbers
    pair, steps_q = two_sum_quadratic(nums, 7_994)       # only the last two add up to it
    pair2, steps_h = two_sum(nums, 7_994)
    print(f"two-sum over 2,000 numbers: {pair} in {steps_q:,} comparisons; {pair2} in {steps_h:,} lookups")
    for n in (10_000, 20_000):
        as_list, as_set = list(range(n)), set(range(n))
        t_list = min(timeit.repeat(lambda: n - 1 in as_list, number=200, repeat=5)) / 200
        t_set = min(timeit.repeat(lambda: n - 1 in as_set, number=200, repeat=5)) / 200
        print(f"  'x in' for n={n:,}: list {t_list * 1e6:.1f} us, set {t_set * 1e9:.0f} ns")

modules.title: Stacks, queues and linked lists
modules.summary: Use stacks and queues for the problems they fit, build a linked list to practise pointer manipulation, and learn the two-pointer and sliding-window techniques that turn quadratic scans into linear ones.

lessons.title: Stacks and queues
objectives: Choose between a stack and a queue for a problem
Implement them with Python's list and collections.deque
Solve bracket matching and next-greater-element problems with a stack
key_points: A stack is last in, first out (LIFO): push and pop at the same end. A Python list makes a good stack, since append and pop() at the end are O(1).
A queue is first in, first out (FIFO): add at the back and remove from the front. collections.deque does both in O(1); list.pop(0) is O(n), because every remaining element shifts.

Stacks fit nesting and undoing: matching brackets (push each opener, and pop and compare at each closer), evaluating expressions, back buttons, and the call stack itself, which is why very deep recursion raises RecursionError.
Queues fit work in arrival order: breadth-first search, task scheduling and buffering between a producer and a consumer. queue.Queue adds blocking put and get for producer and consumer threads.

A monotonic stack keeps its items in increasing or decreasing order by popping those that break the order. It finds every element's next greater element in O(n) in total, because each element is pushed once and popped at most once.
Python's heapq module gives a priority queue, in which the smallest item leaves first rather than the oldest.

lessons.title: Linked lists
objectives: Implement a singly linked list with insertion, removal and reversal
Compare linked lists with arrays
Use fast and slow pointers to find the middle node or a cycle
key_points: A singly linked list is a chain of nodes, each holding a value and a reference to the next node; a doubly linked list also links each node to the previous one. The list keeps a reference to its head, and often to its tail.
Inserting or removing at a node you already hold is O(1), because only references change; but reaching the k-th node takes k steps, as there's no indexing, so searching and access are O(n).

Reverse a singly linked list in place by walking it once and pointing each node's next reference back at the previous node, keeping three references: previous, current and next. It takes O(n) time and O(1) extra space.
A sentinel (dummy) node removes special cases: with a dummy in front of the head, removing the first node is handled by the same code as removing any other.

Fast and slow pointers: move one two steps and the other one step at a time. When the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow one is at the middle; if the list has a cycle, the two meet (Floyd's algorithm), in O(n) time and O(1) space.

In Python, lists and deques beat linked lists for most jobs, thanks to contiguous memory and C implementations; linked structures earn their place when you hold references to nodes, as in an LRU cache's doubly linked list.

lessons.title: Two pointers and sliding windows
objectives: Solve pair and partition problems with two pointers
Use a sliding window for contiguous subarray and substring problems
Keep a running maximum with a monotonic deque
key_points: On a sorted array, two pointers starting at both ends find a pair with a given sum in O(n): if the pair's sum is too small, move the left pointer right; if it's too big, move the right pointer left.
Two pointers moving the same way remove duplicates in place, merge two sorted lists or partition an array, visiting each element once.

A sliding window keeps a contiguous range: extend its right edge one step at a time, and shrink it from the left while a condition is broken. Each index enters and leaves the window once, so the work is O(n) instead of re-scanning every window.

A fixed-size window updates a running total by adding the element that enters and subtracting the one that leaves; variable windows, such as the longest substring without repeated characters, track counts or last-seen positions in a dict.

A monotonic deque gives the maximum of every window of size k in O(n): keep indices whose values decrease from front to back, drop the front index when it leaves the window, and pop from the back any value smaller than the new one.
Each technique needs structure to exploit: sorted order for two pointers from both ends, and contiguity plus a condition that can be updated step by step for sliding windows.

import random
import timeit
from collections import deque

from linked_list import LinkedList, Node, has_cycle
from problems import balanced, longest_unique, next_greater, pair_with_sum, window_max

if __name__ == "__main__":
    ll = LinkedList([3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6])
    ll.remove(1)
    ll.reverse()
    print(f"linked list after remove(1) and reverse(): {list(ll)}, length {len(ll)}, middle {ll.middle()}")
    a, b, c = Node("a"), Node("b"), Node("c")
    a.next, b.next, c.next = b, c, a
    print(f"cycle a->b->c->a detected: {has_cycle(a)}; straight list: {has_cycle(LinkedList([1, 2, 3]).head)}")
    print(f"balanced: {[balanced(s) for s in ['(a[b]{c})', '([)]', '((', '']]}")
    print(f"next greater of [2, 7, 3, 5, 4, 6, 8]: {next_greater([2, 7, 3, 5, 4, 6, 8])}")
    print(f"pair adding to 15 in [1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11]: {pair_with_sum([1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11], 15)}")
    print(f"longest substring without repeats in 'abcabcbb': {longest_unique('abcabcbb')}, "
          f"in 'pwwkew': {longest_unique('pwwkew')}")
    rng = random.Random(4)
    temps = [rng.randint(10, 35) for _ in range(14)]
    print(f"temperatures {temps}\n  3-day maxima {window_max(temps, 3)}")
    for n in (20_000, 40_000):
        t_list = timeit.timeit(lambda: [q.pop(0) for q in [list(range(n))] for _ in range(n)], number=1)
        t_deque = timeit.timeit(lambda: [q.popleft() for q in [deque(range(n))] for _ in range(n)], number=1)
        print(f"  emptying {n:,} items from the front: list.pop(0) {t_list * 1000:.0f} ms, "
              f"deque.popleft() {t_deque * 1000:.1f} ms")

import random

from linked_list import LinkedList, Node, has_cycle
from problems import balanced, longest_unique, next_greater, pair_with_sum, window_max


def test_remove_keeps_head_tail_and_size():
    ll = LinkedList([1, 2, 3, 2])
    assert ll.remove(1) and list(ll) == [2, 3, 2] and ll.head.value == 2
    assert ll.remove(2) and list(ll) == [3, 2]
    assert ll.remove(2) and list(ll) == [3] and ll.tail.value == 3
    assert not ll.remove(99) and len(ll) == 1
    ll.append(4)
    assert list(ll) == [3, 4]


def test_reverse_and_middle():
    ll = LinkedList(range(1, 6))
    ll.reverse()
    assert list(ll) == [5, 4, 3, 2, 1] and ll.tail.value == 1
    ll.append(0)
    assert list(ll)[-1] == 0
    assert LinkedList([1, 2, 3]).middle() == 2 and LinkedList([1, 2, 3, 4]).middle() == 3
    empty = LinkedList()
    empty.reverse()
    assert list(empty) == []


def test_has_cycle():
    nodes = [Node(i) for i in range(5)]
    for x, y in zip(nodes, nodes[1:]):
        x.next = y
    assert not has_cycle(nodes[0])
    nodes[-1].next = nodes[2]
    assert has_cycle(nodes[0])
    assert not has_cycle(None)


def test_balanced():
    assert balanced("{[()()]}") and balanced("no brackets")
    assert not balanced("(]") and not balanced("(()") and not balanced(")(")


def test_next_greater_matches_brute_force():
    rng = random.Random(0)
    nums = [rng.randint(0, 50) for _ in range(200)]
    brute = [next((y for y in nums[i + 1:] if y > x), -1) for i, x in enumerate(nums)]
    assert next_greater(nums) == brute


def test_windows():
    assert longest_unique("abcabcbb") == 3 and longest_unique("bbbb") == 1 and longest_unique("") == 0
    assert longest_unique("abba") == 2
    rng = random.Random(1)
    nums = [rng.randint(-100, 100) for _ in range(300)]
    assert window_max(nums, 7) == [max(nums[i:i + 7]) for i in range(len(nums) - 6)]
    assert pair_with_sum([1, 2, 4, 7], 6) == (1, 2) and pair_with_sum([1, 2], 9) is None

hints: In remove, compare prev.next.value with the value, so prev is always the node before the one you might unlink.
After reverse, the old head is the new tail: set self.tail before the loop moves anything.
In window_max, compare the front index with i - k: the index i - k has just left the window.

modules.title: Trees and heaps
modules.summary: Work with hierarchical data: traverse binary trees recursively and iteratively, keep data searchable in a binary search tree, and use binary heaps, and Python's heapq, as priority queues.

lessons.title: Binary trees and traversals
objectives: Describe binary trees and their vocabulary
Traverse a tree in pre-order, in-order, post-order and level order
Write tree algorithms recursively and iteratively
key_points: A binary tree is made of nodes with at most two children, left and right. The top node is the root, nodes without children are leaves, a node's depth is its distance from the root, and the tree's height is the number of levels on its longest root-to-leaf path.

Depth-first traversals visit a node before its subtrees (pre-order), between them (in-order) or after them (post-order); breadth-first, or level-order, traversal visits the tree level by level with a queue. Each visits every node once: O(n).
Many tree algorithms are a short recursion: levels(None) = 0 and levels(node) = 1 + max(levels(left), levels(right)); counting nodes, summing values and mirroring a tree have the same shape.

Recursion depth equals the tree's height, and CPython's default recursion limit is about 1,000 frames, so a degenerate tree shaped like a linked list can raise RecursionError; an explicit stack or queue avoids it.

Pre-order suits copying or serialising a tree (parents before children), post-order suits values that depend on the children (sizes, heights, freeing a tree), and in-order visits a binary search tree's keys in sorted order.

A complete binary tree, filled level by level from the left, fits in an array with no pointers: the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and its parent at (i − 1) // 2. Binary heaps use this layout.

lessons.title: Binary search trees
objectives: Search, insert and delete in a binary search tree
Explain why balance decides a binary search tree's performance
Choose between a binary search tree, a sorted list and a dict in Python
key_points: A binary search tree keeps every key in a node's left subtree smaller than the node's key and every key in its right subtree larger, so a search goes left or right at each node and visits at most one node per level.
Search and insertion cost O(h) for a tree of height h: O(log n) when the tree is balanced, but O(n) when keys arrive in sorted order and the tree degenerates into a chain.
Deleting a node with two children replaces its key with its in-order successor (the smallest key in its right subtree) and deletes the successor instead, which has at most one child.

Self-balancing trees such as AVL and red-black trees rotate nodes during insertions and deletions to keep the height O(log n) in the worst case; databases use the related B-tree, with many keys per node.
An in-order traversal yields the keys in sorted order, and a search tree answers ordered questions a hash table can't: the smallest key, the next larger key, or every key in a range.

Python has no built-in balanced tree: use a dict for exact lookups, the bisect module on a sorted list for ordered queries with few updates (each insertion is O(n)), or a third-party sorted container when you need both.

lessons.title: Heaps and priority queues
objectives: Explain the heap property and a binary heap's array layout
Implement sift-up and sift-down, and state their costs
Use heapq for priority queues, top-k selection and merging
key_points: A binary min-heap is a complete binary tree in which every parent is less than or equal to its children, so the smallest item is always at the root, index 0 of the array.

Push appends the item and sifts it up, swapping it with its parent while it's smaller; pop moves the last item to the root and sifts it down, swapping it with its smaller child. Both are O(log n), and reading the minimum is O(1).
heapify builds a heap from n items in O(n), not O(n log n): it sifts down every parent from the last one back to the root, and the many nodes near the bottom have little distance to travel.

Python's heapq treats a plain list as a min-heap: heappush, heappop, heapify, heappushpop and heapreplace. For a max-heap, push negated keys; to order other objects, push tuples (priority, counter, item) so that ties never compare the items themselves.

Top-k: keep a min-heap of the k largest items seen so far, replacing the root whenever a larger item arrives, in O(n log k); heapq.nlargest and nsmallest do this for you, and heapq.merge merges sorted inputs lazily.

Priority queues drive Dijkstra's algorithm, event simulations and schedulers. A heap can't search or delete arbitrary items quickly, so mark entries as stale and skip them when they're popped (lazy deletion).

modules.summary: Model networks as graphs, explore them breadth-first and depth-first, put tasks in order with topological sort, and find the shortest weighted routes with Dijkstra's algorithm.

lessons.title: Representing graphs, and breadth-first search
objectives: Represent a graph as an adjacency list or an adjacency matrix
Run breadth-first search to find shortest paths in unweighted graphs
Rebuild a path from a predecessor map
key_points: A graph has vertices and edges; edges can be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted. Road maps, ferry routes, friendships, web links and task dependencies are all graphs.

An adjacency list maps each vertex to its neighbours (in Python, a dict of lists, sets or dicts of weights) and uses O(V + E) memory, suiting sparse graphs; an adjacency matrix uses O(V²) memory but answers 'is there an edge?' in O(1), suiting dense ones.

Breadth-first search (BFS) explores from a source in rings: every vertex one edge away, then two, and so on, using a FIFO queue (collections.deque) and a record of the vertices seen. It runs in O(V + E).

BFS finds shortest paths by number of edges in unweighted graphs: the first time it reaches a vertex, it has reached it by a shortest path. Record each vertex's predecessor, and walk back from the target to rebuild the path.
Mark a vertex as seen when it's added to the queue, not when it's taken off, or the same vertex can be queued many times.
A grid is a graph too: each open cell is a vertex joined to its open neighbours, so BFS solves mazes and flood fills.

lessons.title: Depth-first search and topological sort
objectives: Run depth-first search recursively and with an explicit stack
Find connected components and detect cycles
Put tasks in order with topological sort
key_points: Depth-first search (DFS) follows one path as far as it can before backtracking, recursively or with an explicit stack; like BFS it is O(V + E), but it doesn't find shortest paths.
Starting a search from every vertex not yet seen finds the connected components of an undirected graph: each search marks one component.

In a directed graph, DFS finds a cycle when it reaches a vertex still on the current path (in progress, not finished); in an undirected graph, reaching any visited vertex other than the one you came from means a cycle.

A topological order lists a directed acyclic graph's vertices so that every edge points from earlier to later: course prerequisites, build steps, spreadsheet formulas. One exists only if there's no cycle.

Kahn's algorithm repeatedly removes a vertex with no remaining incoming edges (in-degree 0), using a queue; if vertices remain when the queue is empty, the graph has a cycle. The reverse of a DFS post-order is also a topological order.
Python's standard library has graphlib.TopologicalSorter (since Python 3.9), which raises CycleError for a graph with a cycle.

lessons.title: Dijkstra's algorithm and weighted shortest paths
objectives: Run Dijkstra's algorithm with a priority queue
Explain why Dijkstra's algorithm needs non-negative weights
Choose between BFS, Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford and A*
key_points: Dijkstra's algorithm finds shortest paths from one source when every edge weight is non-negative: it repeatedly settles the unsettled vertex with the smallest known distance and relaxes its edges (if dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v] and its predecessor).
With a binary heap, push (distance, vertex) whenever a distance improves, and skip popped entries for vertices already settled (lazy deletion); the cost is O((V + E) log V).

A settled vertex can't get closer later, because any other path to it passes through a vertex at least as far away and weights can't make a path shorter. A single negative edge breaks that argument, and Dijkstra's algorithm can return wrong distances.
Bellman-Ford handles negative weights by relaxing every edge V − 1 times, in O(V·E), and detects negative cycles: if one more pass still improves a distance, a negative cycle is reachable.

A* adds an estimate of the remaining distance to the priority (f = g + h); with an admissible heuristic that never overestimates, such as straight-line distance on a map, it still finds a shortest path while exploring fewer vertices.
Choose by the graph: BFS for unweighted edges, Dijkstra for non-negative weights, Bellman-Ford when weights can be negative, and A* when there's one target and a good heuristic.

modules.title: Sorting, searching, recursion and dynamic programming
modules.summary: Understand how the main sorting algorithms work and when Python's built-in sort is the answer, search sorted data and monotonic questions with binary search, and solve problems with recursion, memoisation and dynamic programming.

lessons.title: Sorting algorithms
objectives: Explain how merge sort and quicksort work, and what they cost
Explain stability and use it to sort by several keys
Sort with Python's built-in sort and key functions
key_points: A comparison sort needs Ω(n log n) comparisons in the worst case, because it must tell apart all n! orderings and each comparison has two outcomes. Simple sorts (insertion, selection, bubble) are O(n²), though insertion sort is fast on small or nearly sorted inputs.
Merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half recursively and merges the halves in linear time: O(n log n) in every case, and stable, but it needs O(n) extra memory.

Quicksort partitions around a pivot (smaller items to one side, larger to the other) and sorts each side: O(n log n) on average and in place, but O(n²) when the pivot is always extreme, as when the first item is chosen from sorted input. Random or median-of-three pivots avoid that in practice.
A stable sort keeps items with equal keys in their original order, so sorting by a secondary key and then by the primary key sorts by both. Python's sort is stable.

Python's list.sort() and sorted() use Timsort, a hybrid of merge sort and insertion sort that exploits runs already in order: O(n log n) in the worst case and close to O(n) on nearly sorted data. Pass key=, such as key=len or operator.itemgetter(1), rather than writing comparisons.
Counting sort and radix sort don't compare items: for integers in a small range of size k, counting sort is O(n + k).

lessons.title: Binary search
objectives: Implement binary search without off-by-one errors
Use the bisect module on sorted lists
Binary-search on the answer to a monotonic question
key_points: Binary search finds a value in a sorted sequence by comparing it with the middle element and discarding half of the range each time: O(log n) steps, about 20 for a million items.

Keep one invariant to avoid off-by-one errors: search the half-open range [lo, hi), take mid = (lo + hi) // 2, and set lo = mid + 1 or hi = mid until lo == hi. Python's integers can't overflow, so (lo + hi) // 2 is safe.

bisect_left(a, x) returns the first position where x could be inserted to keep a sorted (before any equal items) and bisect_right the position after them, so their difference counts the copies of x; insort inserts in order but is O(n) because of the shift.

Binary search works on any yes/no question whose answer flips once as a number grows: the smallest ship capacity that delivers every parcel within D days, or the first bad version in a history, take O(log range) checks.
Since Python 3.10, the bisect functions accept key=, so a list of records can be searched by one field without building a separate list of keys.
Binary search needs sorted data, and sorting costs O(n log n), so it pays off when you search many times; for a single search, a linear scan is O(n) and simpler.

lessons.title: Recursion, divide and conquer, and backtracking
objectives: Write recursive functions with clear base cases
Analyse divide-and-conquer algorithms with recurrences
Solve search problems by backtracking
key_points: A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on smaller instances, and needs a base case that stops the recursion; each active call holds a stack frame, so the depth matters as well as the total number of calls.

Divide and conquer splits a problem into parts, solves them recursively and combines the results. Its cost follows a recurrence: merge sort's T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) gives O(n log n), and binary search's T(n) = T(n/2) + O(1) gives O(log n).
The master theorem solves T(n) = aT(n/b) + O(n^d): O(n^d) if d > log_b a, O(n^d log n) if they are equal, and O(n^(log_b a)) if d < log_b a.

Backtracking builds a solution one choice at a time and abandons a partial solution as soon as it can't succeed: subsets, permutations, N-queens and sudoku. The worst case is still exponential, but pruning cuts most of the search.

Python doesn't optimise tail calls, and its default recursion limit is about 1,000 frames, so rewrite deep recursions with an explicit stack; raising the limit with sys.setrecursionlimit risks crashing the interpreter.

lessons.title: Dynamic programming
objectives: Recognise overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure
Solve problems with memoisation and with bottom-up tables
Reconstruct the solution, not just its value
key_points: Naive recursion can repeat work exponentially: fib(n) = fib(n − 1) + fib(n − 2) recomputes the same values and makes O(φ^n) calls. Memoisation stores each answer the first time it's computed; the functools.cache decorator does it in one line and makes fib O(n).

Dynamic programming applies when a problem has overlapping subproblems and optimal substructure (a best answer is built from best answers to subproblems). Define the state, the recurrence between states, the base cases and an order of evaluation.

Bottom-up DP fills a table in order without recursion: the fewest coins for amount a is 1 + the minimum of best[a − c] over coins c, with best[0] = 0, in O(amount × coins) time. Greedy change-making fails for some coin systems, such as making 6 from coins 1, 3 and 4.

Two-dimensional DP compares sequences: the longest common subsequence and the edit distance fill an (m + 1) × (n + 1) table, each cell from its neighbours, in O(mn) time; keeping only the previous row cuts the memory to O(n).
Store how each cell was chosen, or walk the table back from the final cell, to reconstruct the solution itself, such as which coins or which edits, not only its value.

"""Sorting algorithms that also count their comparisons."""
from __future__ import annotations

import random


def insertion_sort(a: list) -> tuple[list, int]:
    a, comparisons = list(a), 0
    for i in range(1, len(a)):
        x, j = a[i], i - 1
        while j >= 0:
            comparisons += 1
            if a[j] <= x:
                break
            a[j + 1] = a[j]
            j -= 1
        a[j + 1] = x
    return a, comparisons


def merge(left: list, right: list) -> tuple[list, int]:

def merge_sort(a: list) -> tuple[list, int]:

    left, c1 = merge_sort(a[:mid])

def quicksort(a: list, pivot: str = "first", seed: int = 0) -> tuple[list, int]:
    """Quicksort with an explicit stack of ranges, so a bad pivot can't overflow Python's recursion limit.
    pivot='first' uses each range's first item; 'random' a random one (seeded). The chosen pivot is swapped to
    the end of the range before partitioning."""
    a, comparisons = list(a), 0
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    stack = [(0, len(a) - 1)]
    while stack:
        lo, hi = stack.pop()
        if lo >= hi:
            continue
        p = lo if pivot == "first" else rng.randint(lo, hi)
        a[p], a[hi] = a[hi], a[p]
        mid, c = partition(a, lo, hi)
        comparisons += c
        stack.append((lo, mid - 1))
        stack.append((mid + 1, hi))
    return a, comparisons

project.brief: A city's transit authority wants a journey planner that is fast and demonstrably correct. make_network.py generates its network: stops, the edges between consecutive stops on each line with travel minutes, every departure of every line at every stop, and 20,000 passenger tap-ins. Build planner.py, a library with a small command-line interface, and test it with pytest. It must load the network into an adjacency list; find the route with the fewest rides between two stops (BFS) and the fastest one (Dijkstra, ignoring waiting time); find the next departure from a stop after a given time with binary search over each stop's sorted timetable; list the ten busiest stops from the tap-ins with a heap; and work out the cheapest way to buy at least N rides from single tickets (2.00), 10-ride packs (18.00) and 30-ride packs (50.00) with dynamic programming. As a stretch, compute the earliest arrival with waiting included, using a time-dependent Dijkstra that waits for the next departure at each stop. On the default network your planner should report that S001 to S060 takes three rides and 13 minutes, that the next departure from S001 after 08:00 is line L3 (out) at 08:01, that the busiest stops are S014, S033 and S024, and that 47 rides cost 82.00. Then measure it: generate networks with --stops 200, 400 and 800 (and lines to match), time each operation, and compare the growth with your analysis.

"""Generate a transit network for the journey planner (same files for the same arguments).

python make_network.py                       60 stops, 6 lines: the network the brief's answers refer to
python make_network.py --stops 400 --lines 30 --out big    a larger one, for doubling benchmarks

Writes, in the output folder:
  stops.csv       stop_id,name
  edges.csv       from,to,line,minutes          (one row per direction)
  departures.csv  stop_id,line,direction,time    (HH:MM, every trip of every line at every stop)
  taps.csv        stop_id,time                   (passengers tapping in)
"""
import argparse
import csv
import random
from pathlib import Path


def main() -> None:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--stops", type=int, default=60)
    ap.add_argument("--lines", type=int, default=6)
    ap.add_argument("--taps", type=int, default=20_000)
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=2026)
    ap.add_argument("--out", default="network")
    args = ap.parse_args()
    rng = random.Random(args.seed)
    out = Path(args.out)
    out.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    stops = [f"S{i:03d}" for i in range(1, args.stops + 1)]
    with open(out / "stops.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["stop_id", "name"])
        w.writerows([s, f"Stop {s[1:]}"] for s in stops)
    routes = {}
    for n in range(1, args.lines + 1):
        line = f"L{n}"
        k = rng.randint(10, 15)
        # every line after the first shares at least one stop with an earlier line, so the network is connected
        start = rng.choice([s for r in routes.values() for s in r]) if routes else rng.choice(stops)
        path = [start] + rng.sample([s for s in stops if s != start], k - 1)
        routes[line] = path
    edges, departures = [], []
    for line, path in routes.items():
        minutes = [rng.randint(2, 6) for _ in path[:-1]]
        headway = rng.choice([10, 12, 15, 20])
        for direction, seq, mins in (("out", path, minutes), ("back", path[::-1], minutes[::-1])):
            for a, b, m in zip(seq, seq[1:], mins):
                edges.append([a, b, line, m])
            for first in range(5 * 60 + 30, 23 * 60 + 31, headway):
                t = first
                for i, stop in enumerate(seq):
                    departures.append([stop, line, direction, f"{t // 60:02d}:{t % 60:02d}"])
                    if i < len(mins):
                        t += mins[i]
    with open(out / "edges.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["from", "to", "line", "minutes"])
        w.writerows(edges)
    departures.sort(key=lambda r: (r[0], r[1], r[2], r[3]))
    with open(out / "departures.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["stop_id", "line", "direction", "time"])
        w.writerows(departures)
    served = sorted({s for p in routes.values() for s in p})
    weights = [rng.paretovariate(1.2) for _ in served]          # a few stops are far busier than the rest
    with open(out / "taps.csv", "w", newline="") as f:
        w = csv.writer(f)
        w.writerow(["stop_id", "time"])
        for stop in rng.choices(served, weights=weights, k=args.taps):
            t = rng.randint(5 * 60 + 30, 23 * 60 + 30)
            w.writerow([stop, f"{t // 60:02d}:{t % 60:02d}"])
    print(f"{out}/: {len(served)} served stops of {len(stops)}, {len(routes)} lines, {len(edges)} directed edges, "
          f"{len(departures):,} departures, {args.taps:,} taps")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
